paragraphs: Here's what this whole passage is about, friend: God is in charge, and nobody can bargain Him down. Pharaoh tried everything. He said "I have sinned" when the locusts came, then he haggled over who could go and what had to stay behind (Exodus 10:16, 24). God told Moses why He was doing all this: so that parents could "tell your children and grandchildren," and "so that all of you may know that I am the LORD" (Exodus 10:2).

Now look at what Pharaoh's words were missing. He said sorry, but he wanted the plague gone more than he wanted to obey, and the moment it lifted, nothing changed (Exodus 10:19-20). He even said "once more," which means this wasn't the first time he'd said it (Exodus 10:17). That's the difference between being sorry the pain showed up and turning to God. I've heard plenty of promises made at 2 a.m. that didn't survive breakfast, friend, and I'm not pointing fingers because I've made a few myself.

And here's the good news tucked in the dark. While Egypt sat in total darkness, "all the Israelites had light in their dwellings" (Exodus 10:23). God sees His people, and He knows exactly where they are. Moses refused every half deal because God asked for all of it, and that's the question this passage leaves with you: when God says come, are you bringing everything, or just the part that's easy to carry?
